tip: 'A gente' means 'we' but takes a singular verb: 'a gente é,' never 'a gente somos.' It is the everyday spoken 'we.'
Masculine plural covers mixed groups: 'irmãos' means brothers, or siblings of both genders. An all-female set would be 'irmãs.'
'Simpática' means nice or friendly, not 'sympathetic.' It describes a warm, likeable person.
No article before a profession: 'ele é engenheiro,' not 'um engenheiro.' Portuguese drops the 'a/an' that English uses here.
'Fazer aniversário,' literally 'to make a birthday,' is how you say to have a birthday: 'faço aniversário em março.'
'Ir a pé,' literally 'go by foot,' means to walk somewhere: 'a gente pode ir a pé.'
'Dar conta de' means to handle or manage something: 'ela dá conta de tudo.' Literally 'to give account of.'
Days of the week take 'no/na' for 'on': 'no sábado' = on Saturday. There is no separate word for 'on.'
Clock times use 'às': 'às dez' = at ten. It is 'a' plus feminine 'as,' since hours are feminine (as horas).
Transport uses 'ir de': 'vai de Uber' = goes by Uber. Use 'de' for car, bus, or train. The one exception is 'a pé,' on foot.
'Sem' plus an infinitive equals English 'without' plus -ing: 'sem pensar' = without thinking.
'Perguntar' is to ask a question. To ask for something is 'pedir.' Here: 'perguntar para o garçom,' ask the waiter.
Comparatives just add 'mais' before the adjective: 'mais barato' = cheaper. No word ending changes.
